tldr: A slide-free demo tour of DuckDB, from the CLI and JDBC through querying CSV, Parquet, S3 and Postgres in one engine, to DuckLake and the upcoming Quack client-server protocol.
summary: Oliver Geisser presented DuckDB as an open-source, in-process, column-oriented analytical database, fast at aggregations and weak at single-row transactions, and demoed everything live. After the CLI and its dot commands (.databases, .tables, .read), he embedded the engine via plain JDBC in a JBang script, noting DuckDB's own connection class for chunked columnar reads, and from Python. CSV import auto-detects delimiters and types, a 40-million-row Parquet file loaded into memory, and larger-than-memory data spills to disk. The dialect allows FROM 'file.parquet' with no SELECT *. The same file-system layer reads over HTTPS and S3, with credentials held in persistent secrets outside the code.

He attached DuckDB files, SQLite and a remote Postgres to one session so queries can join across them, which led to DuckLake: a standard-SQL catalog plus Parquet files on object storage. He built three lakes: all local, local catalog with S3, and Postgres catalog with S3, the last being a production setup. Multi-user access has needed Postgres because read-write DuckDB locks its file exclusively. With a DuckDB 2.0 alpha he started a server over the new Quack protocol and attached a second CLI with the new CONNECT command to query the S3-backed lake remotely. He said Quack ships at the end of the month.
keyPoints: DuckDB runs in-process as a C++ library behind the CLI, JDBC and Python clients; the JDBC driver adds a chunk-based API for columnar results.
File formats (CSV, JSON, Excel, Parquet, SQLite) are read via extensions with type and delimiter auto-detection, locally, over HTTPS or from S3.
ATTACH lets one DuckDB session join data across DuckDB files, SQLite, Postgres and other databases, translating the dialect for the remote engine.
DuckLake keeps lake metadata in a plain SQL catalog (DuckDB or Postgres) and writes append-only Parquet files to local disk or S3.
The Quack protocol, shown in a DuckDB 2.0 alpha, turns DuckDB into a client-server database so several clients can share one read-write lake.
takeaways: Try DuckDB without installing anything at shell.duckdb.org, which runs on WebAssembly.
Store cloud and database credentials as DuckDB persistent secrets instead of in scripts.
For a cheap lakehouse, evaluate DuckLake with a small Postgres catalog and Parquet on S3 before a managed cloud offering.
watchIf: You need to analyse files or join data from several databases without running a warehouse, or you are weighing a lightweight lakehouse.
